Read the accounts: what Jamie’s Italian taught me about supplier risk

Most supplier reviews look backwards. We check last quarter’s OTIF, quality issues and price. Rarely do we ask whether the supplier will still be able to deliver next year.

By Pupsi Phull4 minute read

Evidence boundary. Published metrics retain their stated source and context. Diagrams are illustrative and contain no client data.

During my MBA, I compared the published accounts of Jamie’s Italian and Carluccio’s in the years before each went into administration. Both still looked busy from the outside. The accounts told a different story: mounting losses, tight cash and fixed costs, mainly leases, that left little room to adapt.

Why this matters in operations

A supplier can hit every service target while its ability to keep doing so is draining away. By the time service slips, your options have narrowed.

You do not need to be an accountant

Three questions cover most of the risk:

  • Is the business generating cash, or burning it?
  • Are its debts and fixed commitments growing faster than its sales?
  • Is it still investing in the equipment and people your supply depends on?

No single ratio predicts failure. The trend over two or three years, and the story behind it, matters more.

What I now do differently

For any supplier that would be hard to replace within three months, I add a financial health check to the annual review, and I agree a fallback route while service is still stable. It costs little, and it is far easier than finding a new supplier in a crisis.

Based on Cranfield Executive MBA research. Views are my own.
